1 big thing: Routing is coming for the frontier AI labs
By Madison Mills
 

Illustration: Aïda Amer/Axios
 

Businesses seeking more affordable and secure ways to use AI are turning to routing — the process of matching each query with the best, most efficient model for the task.

Why it matters: The popularization of routing could stymie the usage of the frontier AI models that are the most expensive to use and make.

State of play: Routing is booming.

  • Stripe agreed to buy unicorn OpenRouter for more than $8 billion, the company announced last week.
  • OpenRouter had 8 million users and 400 models available on the platform as of May, per Bloomberg.
  • Meta is reportedly working on an OpenRouter competitor called Switchboard, per The Information, which the company may use to lower its own AI costs.
  • Even the frontier AI labs have launched model pickers that allow users to select which model or level of intelligence they want to use for a certain task.

How it works: Routing companies say that it's extremely quick and easy to get started. (In a demo, I was able to use a DeepSeek model in under 30 seconds using TrustedRouter, an open-source routing company.)

  • A simple query may call on a smaller flash model, while a complex task could go to a more expensive one.
  • Companies can set their own priorities for the router, including cost, speed, performance and which models or providers they trust with their data.

Flashback: The routing boom was fueled by concerns about AI costs.

  • Usage of open models, which can be cheaper, has skyrocketed: The five most popular models used on OpenRouter are all open weight or open source. OpenAI and Google each have only one model in the top 10, and Anthropic has none.
  • Average token costs have plummeted since a peak in mid-May due to price cuts from frontier AI labs looking to gain back share from their competitors.

Zoom out: There's also a growing push for AI sovereignty, or protecting your enterprise IP and not sharing it with frontier labs, that routers aim to address.

  • "I see people excited about us and moving to us because they don't like what Anthropic is becoming," Joseph Perla, founder of TrustedRouter, told Axios.
  • TrustedRouter is encrypted end to end to make compute "confidential," Perla said.
  • Palantir recently hosted a sovereignty boot camp in NYC packed with speakers, including one who said, "Are we going to throw our years of knowledge to a frontier AI model? Absolutely not."

Reality check: People are not broadly arguing the frontier AI labs are going to die because of model routing.

  • "It's not to say you won't ever use commercial models, but it's like you want to have the options to use models that are specific to you," Akshay Krishnaswamy, chief architect at Palantir, told Axios.
  • Demand for intelligence is such that there can be multiple winners, because these platforms also "put their models in front of more users and more workloads," Matan Grinberg, CEO of Factory AI, a routing company, told Axios.

The bottom line: Routing turns models from destinations in their own right into interchangeable commodities, which could threaten margins for frontier AI models.
 
 
2. Fitbit founders debut band for aging parents
By Ina Fried
 

The Luffu Link band. Image: Luffu
 

Luffu, the startup created by two of Fitbit's co-founders, debuted a fitness band today that they say is part of their effort to tap the power of AI to help family members keep tabs on one another.

Why it matters: The project aims to address the challenges faced by caregivers, including those in the sandwich generation with aging parents and kids at home.

Driving the news: The Luffu Link, which will be available early next year, combines sleep and step tracking with voice recording, location tracking and a cellular modem, all in service of keeping tabs on one's own health and that of family members.

  • The band will cost $299 ($249 for those who preorder).
  • The company won't charge separately for cellular service, but the band requires the company's $20-per-month family subscription plan (covers up to four people).

How it works: Link wearers can press the band's button to record a voice memo that is sent to Luffu's AI-powered service. Messages can include a description of a symptom, a record of medicine taken, other health information or anything else they want to remember.

  • Luffu can use AI to determine things such as missed medications or a change in vitals, but family members control what gets shared with the AI or with loved ones.
  • Users can also use the band to summon help from a family member, while two quick presses of the button sends a message that means all is good.

What they're saying: "The purpose of it is to keep people healthy, safe, independent, but also connected to the people who care about them," Luffu CEO and former Fitbit CEO James Park said in an interview.

What we're watching: Park is also teasing a home device with a screen that will eventually be part of the lineup.
 
 
3. Exclusive: Cisco bets on infrastructure boom
By Madison Mills
 

Cisco president and chief product officer Jeetu Patel. Photo: Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images
 

Cisco is partnering with Supermicro to add high-powered AI servers to its Nvidia-backed infrastructure offering, expanding beyond networking to sell more of the equipment needed to run AI.

Why it matters: Cisco is leaning into its AI infrastructure business, betting that compute demand is not slowing anytime soon.

Driving the news: Cisco is working with Supermicro to add high-density, liquid- and air-cooled computing systems to its Secure AI Factory with Nvidia, the company told Axios.

  • The systems will support Nvidia's next-generation platforms and are expected to become available in October.
